segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Two shots. That's all it took.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Ten past four that Friday morning, crouched behind my own bumper in a hospital garage, I learned what a life ending sounds like in concrete.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I looked over the hood. A man was sliding down the side of a silver sedan, a gun a foot from his open hand. The man standing over him held a different gun, in his left hand. His right arm was in the plaster splint I had built thirty minutes earlier, in bay fourteen, with my own two hands.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Go back inside, Dr. Marlowe. You were never here.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I went back inside. Three days later I married him.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: It started at 3:05 that morning, with a man walking into my ER holding his own arm closed. Half the waiting room went quiet for him. Denise at triage half stood up. The security guard found something interesting on his shoes. Everybody knew a rule about this man. Nobody had told me.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Bay fourteen. A clean cut across the inside of his right forearm. Gray eyes. A thin white scar through his left eyebrow.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Knife?" I asked.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: I'd rather not say what cut it.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Somewhere you need to be?"

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: You've done this before.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "A couple hundred times. Usually on people who tell me their name."

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Nico.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Vescari.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: By 3:40 I had built him a splint of plaster, fingertips to elbow. Six weeks, no gripping. If he grabbed anything hard, that tendon would snap like a rubber band. He set a fold of hundreds on my tray.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: For the chart. There doesn't need to be one.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "There's always a chart." I tucked the money back into his pocket and typed his name while he watched. I said it too hard. He couldn't know why.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Level two, spot 2-14. At 4:08 I found the charger in the cup holder. At 4:10, two shots went off, so close together they sounded like one word. I counted. One, two, three, four. Footsteps. Something heavy hitting a car door. At nine, I looked.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Let me get to him," I said. "I can—"

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: He's gone, Dottoressa. Go.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Behind him, in the stairwell, feet were going down fast. Then they stopped. Someone was standing on those stairs, listening, and those stairs were my only way out. I counted his breaths. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. The next one didn't come. The last time I stood that close to someone dying while other people decided I should stay out of the way, I was fourteen.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: At 4:16 I called 911 and my voice came out steady. By 4:31 the silver sedan was gone, and so was the man. The floor smelled like bleach and fake pine. The camera had been down since Tuesday. A young officer told me a car backfiring sounds like a cannon in concrete.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I had a name on my tongue. I didn't say it. I'm not proud of that.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Saturday at eight, a woman in a rain jacket and a man in a navy suit sat on my couch. Special Agent Reyes. Prosecutor Holloway. A city crew had pulled a man out of the Gowanus Canal. Frankie Lombardi. Two gunshot wounds to the chest. Frankie worked for the Vescari family, and also, quietly, for the FBI. That made his murder a federal case, and me its witness.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I told them in order, like presenting a patient. Two shots at 4:10. Nico standing over a man by a silver car, a gun in his left hand, my splint on his right. Notice what I didn't say: that I saw anyone fire. I heard two shots. I saw what came after.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Holloway left a subpoena. Thursday, ten a.m. He offered a new name, a new city, witness protection. I laughed. I had nine months of residency left. I wasn't becoming a dental hygienist in Tucson because a man in a nice suit told me to go back inside.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "I'll tell them," I said. "But I'm doing it as myself."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: At seven that night I carried groceries up three flights and found my door unlocked and my lamp off. Nico Vescari sat in my mother's armchair in the dark, my splint resting on the arm. My little brother sat beside him, white as paper. "Ivy," Theo said. "I'm so sorry."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Forty thousand dollars, a betting app, then interest. Theo was crying the way he did at fifteen, when he thought I couldn't hear through the wall.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: His bookie works for Carmine Brancato, who wants my port. If you die before Thursday, with my name in your statement, nobody needs a trial.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "So someone wants me dead, and it isn't you."

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: It isn't me.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Did you kill that man?"

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: I'm not going to answer that.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Marry me. A wife can't be forced to testify against her husband. The privilege belongs to the wife. Not to me. Not to Holloway.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I laughed. "I met you on Friday. You bled on my shoes. Here's my answer." I held up the subpoena. "I'd rather testify."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Sunday, a man in bay seventeen asked for the redheaded doctor. In the supply room the door clicked shut and IV tubing dropped over my head. You get about ten seconds before you pass out. I teach that to students. At five I drove my trauma shears into the back of his hand, and he ran.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: A huge man filled the doorway, the quiet one with the crossword. Rocco. "Go after him," I croaked.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "No, ma'am. My job's you."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: That evening I stood by my car with a red line round my throat. I could become someone else in a city I'd never seen, or keep my work and my brother and trust a man I didn't. I was scared of him. I was more scared of a plastic tube. He answered on the first ring.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "I have conditions," I said.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: His lawyer wrote it down in blue ink. One. I keep my residency, every shift. Two. My own bedroom, with a lock on my side. Three. Theo's debt, gone tonight. Four. No one in his family touches me, including his men. Five. When the case is dead, we divorce. Six. Not one cent of his money.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "And seven. You never lie to me."

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: I'll never lie to you. I won't always answer.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "That's a loophole."

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: That's the truth. You asked for the truth.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Is it the only reason you want this? If I can't testify, you're safe?"

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "What's the other one?"

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: He held my eyes and said nothing at all. Beside him, Tommy looked at the table. Whatever it was, Tommy knew.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: My uncle Sal came at one-thirty with a box of cannoli and sugar on his tie. My father's brother, his consigliere for twenty-five years, and now mine.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: "You're a better man than your father was," Sal said. "But a better man makes trouble for himself. A girl in the house with a federal subpoena. It would be cleaner, Nico, the other way."

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: We don't touch civilians. That's the only thing that makes us different from Brancato. Take that away and we're just men with guns who like the port.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: He held up both hands, cannoli in one. "I had to say it so you could say no. That's my job." Then he went out to the garden for air and left the door open behind him.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Eleven pages, typed overnight. At the bottom of Nico's section, someone had added a line by hand in big, shaky, left-handed capitals. She will look like she loves me. I initialed it. I read every page twice.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: The ring was his grandmother's, a square emerald, far too big. It slid around my finger. "Rosa had big hands," he said. "She made bread."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: On the courthouse steps, eight reporters and three cameras. Holloway had been tipped. Nico kissed me, slow and warm, the plaster along my spine. It was for the cameras. For three seconds I forgot to count anything, and I was angry about that all day.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Starting tonight, Dottoressa, we're in love.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: He had put a bolt on my side of the connecting door himself, at six that morning, left-handed. The screws were crooked. I tested it four times. The ring was so loose it kept turning to my palm.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Tuesday, the ER. At work I couldn't wear a ring under gloves, so I'd threaded his grandmother's emerald onto a thin gold chain and tucked it under my scrubs. A wedding ring that lived against my breastbone. Joey, one of Nico's soldiers, rolled in stabbed, lung collapsing. I decompressed him and put in the tube myself while mobsters watched me do it. "Am I dead?" he asked. "Not on my shift."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: In his jacket I found my whole October. Every shift in blue ballpoint, small neat slanted handwriting I didn't know. And at the bottom, underlined twice: Level 2. Space 2-14.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Joey said the man who sent him drove a car that smelled like anise. Only the hospital had my schedule. Dr. Bell had asked about my shifts that morning, almost casually. I told myself Bell asks everybody everything.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I confronted Bell Thursday evening. He cried. His son Danny was seventeen and sick, and the treatment cost four hundred seventy thousand dollars. A man had asked about my schedule. Bell gave it. I gave him until noon to call the FBI. He asked for one more night. I said yes. I have thought about that yes every day since.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: That night I was shaking, and he held me, and he pulled the pen out of my hair with his left hand. I kissed him. He kissed me back. I stopped. No cameras. "That one wasn't for anyone," I said. "Sleep," he said. "I'll wake you at eleven."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: At 6:41 Friday morning, Priya called. Dr. Bell was dead in his Volvo, three spaces from my spot. A note on his phone. Suicide. "Ivy, I'm sorry. I couldn't live with it. Tell Danny I tried."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: In three years Bell called me Ivy maybe four times, always when someone had just died. In writing, always Marlowe, even in his last text. The note was a lie, and whoever wrote it didn't know him.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Only four people had known he'd talk to the FBI at noon. Nico. Tommy. Rocco. And Nico's uncle Sal. When I said that name aloud, Nico's eyes dropped to the top drawer of his desk, for as long as it takes to read a clock.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Sunday lunch under the fig. Enzo excused himself and didn't come back. I found him on his bathroom floor, blue, a foil card beside him. Oxycodone, thirty milligrams. I breathed for him. Two sprays of naloxone, three minutes apart. He gasped. I put the card in my cardigan pocket before the paramedics came. I only knew it mattered.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: In the ER, Enzo grabbed my sleeve and told me, because he thought he was dying. "I shot him. I shot Frankie."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: He had followed Frankie into the garage and stood half a flight up the stairs, holding his breath. A shoe scraped. Frankie turned, and his gun came up. Enzo fired twice and didn't even decide to. Nico took the gun out of his hand and told him to go.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Enzo was the light jacket on the stairs. He had stopped when he heard me ask for a tube. Then he kept going. I told him what he said in that bay stays with me. I didn't know yet what it would cost.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Then Theo was arrested. Four hundred tablets, taped under the driver's seat of his Civic. Holloway offered a trade: my testimony against Nico, and Theo walks. Nico, in the car, never raised his voice. "Do what you have to do. I won't hate you."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I had my own evidence. The sticker on Enzo's card said Lot 4471-B. So did the pills in Theo's car. I cornered the hospital pharmacy director with an old committee letter. Forty-two cards of that lot had been "destroyed" on a form dated September twenty-ninth, co-signed by Dr. Marcus Bell. The tech said nobody counted. The signing doctor carried the bag out himself, past the garage.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Nico's people found the dealer. His supplier was an old man in a gray Lincoln that smelled of licorice.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Monday, Courtroom 6B. Holloway wanted the judge to call it a sham marriage. He called me to the stand and asked about the first week. About the courthouse kiss. And I invited him to ask the real question.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Do you love your husband?"

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Yes. I love him. And I'd like the record to show he's hearing it for the first time with everyone else."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: The judge denied the motion from the bench. She'd seen a great many sham marriages, and none of them sounded like that. In the car, Nico's left hand lay open on the seat, palm up. I put mine in it. At my door he said, "One day, when you're ready, and not before, I'd like to hear it once without them."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: At midnight I couldn't sleep. Holloway had asked me that morning, "Eleven pages?" Only I, Nico, Mr. Feld and one copy in Nico's top drawer knew how many pages the contract had. Someone inside the house was talking to the government's side. I opened the drawer. Under the paper, a white twist of candy wrapper. It smelled of anise.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: One-ten in the morning, in my uncle's garage. I had found this car once before and told myself Brancato might be framing him. Half of Brooklyn sucks anise candy. This time I opened the glove box. A black ledger, its band off with my teeth because I only had one hand. C.B., every month for four years, starting the week of my father's funeral. And on the first of October: F.L. Twenty. Paid.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: In the trunk, a deli receipt for a prepaid phone, and a boy's tan jacket from a discount rack. When I was eleven, my father broke my nose, and Sal carried me out of that house.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: She was sitting in my study with the candy twist in her hand. I said it before she could. It's my uncle.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: At dawn, Danny Bell let me read his father's last letter. Marcus had signed the destruction form and carried the pills to a gray car for cash. Years ago he'd misdiagnosed a patient who turned out to be Brancato's cousin, and Brancato had held it over him ever since. The man in the gray car was old, soft-spoken, nice coat. The letter ended: Ivy, say it. Say all of it. Danny said I could give it to the FBI. I gave Reyes everything except one name. "Somebody else gets to tell you first," I said.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Tuesday, seven p.m. Sal arrived exactly on time with a box of pastry. Nico laid out the notebook, the receipt, the jacket. Sal didn't blink. "Carmine wanted the port," he said, "and the port was you. Frankie lost his nerve. I didn't know about the stairs. I didn't know Carmine's boy would send Enzo down them."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Kids buy pills," he said. "Better ours, from a hospital, clean, than poison pressed in a bathtub in Jersey."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I broke my own rule and spoke. "I breathed for your nephew for four minutes, Mr. Vescari. On your pills."

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: My father would have put you in the water, Zio. That's the answer I'm not giving anymore. You'll go to Cefalù. Everything you own goes to Frankie's kids, Michael and Gina.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Sal looked at his hands, then at his nephew. "Somebody in this family had to be his father. You were busy being a saint."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I put my phone on the tablecloth and called Agent Reyes on speaker. Sal almost smiled. "Of course you called her, sweetheart. You always do."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: A day later I chained a deli receipt and a pack of gum to Paulie Ferraro. I called Reyes first, on purpose. Then Nico.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Three weeks ago, I'd have sent Tommy. I trust what you'd do.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Paulie confessed. Theo walked out at 12:52. In the car he said, "You never once asked me if I wanted to be your kid." I'd been so busy keeping him safe that I'd never asked. I asked.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Monday night Lucia found Enzo's room empty. At 11:31 my phone rang. Carmine Brancato. His own son had overdosed on the floor of his club, and Enzo, who'd walked in to offer himself for a boy he'd hit on a bicycle four years ago, had asked for the doctor. I didn't ask permission. I told everyone before, not after. I texted Reyes. I went.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Enzo was already breathing for him. I gave naloxone and bagged him. Four minutes twenty seconds. The boy coughed. Brancato took a typed statement out of his cardigan. I, Enzo Vescari, state that my brother ordered me to. Enzo wouldn't sign it. "I'll sign what's true. I won't sign that."

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: I'm not armed, Carmine. My wife doesn't like it.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Six guns turned. I stepped in front of him. "Be quiet. It's my turn." I told Brancato what I'd tell a jury. His son was breathing because of me. If anyone fired, I would stand in a courtroom and say who. He said, "In my house, we don't point guns at the doctor." He told them to put them down.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Reyes came through the front door two minutes later with a warrant signed at six. She arrested Carmine Brancato.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: I came in with nothing because you were in that room. That's the truth, Ivy.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Enzo turned himself in at two-fourteen Tuesday morning. In the visiting room I said, I'm sorry I made you carry it, and I cried in front of a guard. Then I went to Holloway about the gun, buried in the planter on Van Brunt Street under the geraniums. I told Feld to draw an uncontested divorce and leave it on the hall table. She gets to choose once with nothing on the table. That means I don't ask.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Thursday, third grand jury. I waived my privilege myself, that morning at six, for October third and nothing else. I told them what I saw. Two shots at 4:10. A man sliding down a silver car. A second gun near his open hand. Nico standing over him with a gun in his left hand, pointed at the floor, held wrong, and his right hand in my splint.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "Did you see who fired?"

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: "No. I heard two shots. I saw what was in his hands afterward."

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Holloway told us in the hallway there'd be no indictment for Frankie Lombardi: Enzo's statement, my testimony, Frankie's gun, the chart. Nico would plead to tampering with a gun. At two o'clock I took off the splint, six weeks less one day. His fist closed. All of it, even the ring finger I sewed. He looked at his own hand a long time.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Thank you, Dr. Marlowe.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: That evening there was a cream envelope on the hall table. Term Five. Three stapled pages. He'd signed it with his right hand, slowly, like a man writing in a foreign language. I put the papers down and went upstairs.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I didn't knock. "Here's the thing about the divorce," I said. "I haven't asked." I emptied my cardigan pockets onto his bed: Enzo's foil card, the pharmacy form, his note, Bell's envelope, a candy twist. Everything I'd carried through five weeks. I took the pen out of my hair. On page eleven, under his left-handed line, I wrote, She does. And under that: Term six. Nobody in this house is quiet anymore.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: Last March a woman buried her son from my house on Carroll Street. Rosaria Amato. She told me about a red-haired doctor at St. Brigid's who sat with her and told her the truth. She said your name twice. I read Marlowe on your badge, and I chose that emergency room. That was the other reason.

segments.speaker: lion
segments.text: I love you, Ivy. I've loved you since you put my money back in my pocket and typed my name anyway.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: April. The lemon trees came out of their burlap. "It's a lemon tree," Lucia said. "It's Sicilian. It lives out of spite. Like me." Theo has an apartment over a laundromat and comes for Saturday lunch and calls me Iv. Enzo is in a program upstate, a hundred forty-one days clean, writing to his mother on Sundays and to a boy named Anthony who hasn't answered yet. Sal's letters from Cefalù, Lucia burns unread. Danny Bell is back at school; an anonymous donor paid his treatment. When I asked, Nico said, "I'm not going to answer that," and smiled. I finish residency in June.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: Reyes came to the gate on the first warm Saturday. A motion from Brancato's lawyers had surfaced old files. Nico's father had been an FBI informant for years. Nico would read it in the Post by Friday.

segments.speaker: heba
segments.text: I did not wait. We don't do silence in this house anymore. It's in the contract. I climbed fourteen stairs, counting every one, to tell my husband the truth about his father. Two shots. That's all it took to start all of this. One yes, said out loud, is how it ended.

chapters.title: What I Saw, And What I Didn't

captions.text: Two shots. That's all it took.
Ten past four that Friday morning,

crouched behind my own
bumper in a hospital garage,

I learned what a life ending
sounds like in concrete.
I looked over the hood.

A man was sliding down the side of a silver
sedan, a gun a foot from his open hand.

The man standing over him held a
different gun, in his left hand.

His right arm was in the plaster splint
I had built thirty minutes earlier,
in bay fourteen, with my own two hands.
Go back inside, Dr. Marlowe.
You were never here.
I went back inside.
Three days later I married him.
It started at 3:05 that morning,

with a man walking into my ER
holding his own arm closed.
Half the waiting room went quiet for him.
Denise at triage half stood up.

The security guard found something
interesting on his shoes.
Everybody knew a rule about this man.
Nobody had told me.
Bay fourteen.

A clean cut across the
inside of his right forearm.
Gray eyes.
A thin white scar through his left eyebrow.
"Knife?" I asked.
I'd rather not say what cut it.
"Somewhere you need to be?"
You've done this before.
"A couple hundred times.
Usually on people who tell me their name."
Nico.
Vescari.

By 3:40 I had built him a splint
of plaster, fingertips to elbow.
Six weeks, no gripping.

If he grabbed anything hard, that
tendon would snap like a rubber band.
He set a fold of hundreds on my tray.
For the chart.
There doesn't need to be one.

"There's always a chart." I tucked the
money back into his pocket and typed his
name while he watched. I said it too hard.
He couldn't know why.
Level two, spot 2-14.

At 4:08 I found the
charger in the cup holder.

At 4:10, two shots went off, so close
together they sounded like one word.
I counted. One, two, three, four.
Footsteps.
Something heavy hitting a car door.
At nine, I looked.
"Let me get to him," I said. "I can—"
He's gone, Dottoressa. Go.

Behind him, in the stairwell,
feet were going down fast.
Then they stopped.

Someone was standing on
those stairs, listening,
and those stairs were my only way out.
I counted his breaths. Seven. Eight. Nine.
Ten. The next one didn't come.

The last time I stood that close to
someone dying while other people decided I
should stay out of the way, I was fourteen.

At 4:16 I called 911 and
my voice came out steady.

By 4:31 the silver sedan was
gone, and so was the man.
The floor smelled like bleach and fake pine.
The camera had been down since Tuesday.

A young officer told me a car backfiring
sounds like a cannon in concrete.
I had a name on my tongue.
I didn't say it. I'm not proud of that.

Saturday at eight, a woman in a rain
jacket and a man in a navy suit sat on my
couch. Special Agent Reyes.
Prosecutor Holloway.

A city crew had pulled a man
out of the Gowanus Canal.
Frankie Lombardi.
Two gunshot wounds to the chest.

Frankie worked for the Vescari family,
and also, quietly, for the FBI.

That made his murder a federal
case, and me its witness.

I told them in order, like
presenting a patient.
Two shots at 4:10.

Nico standing over a man by a
silver car, a gun in his left hand,
my splint on his right.

Notice what I didn't say:
that I saw anyone fire.
I heard two shots. I saw what came after.
Holloway left a subpoena.
Thursday, ten a.m.

He offered a new name, a new
city, witness protection.
I laughed.
I had nine months of residency left.

I wasn't becoming a dental hygienist in
Tucson because a man in a nice suit told me
to go back inside.
"I'll tell them," I said.
"But I'm doing it as myself."

At seven that night I carried groceries up
three flights and found my door unlocked
and my lamp off.

Nico Vescari sat in my mother's armchair
in the dark, my splint resting on the arm.

My little brother sat
beside him, white as paper.
"Ivy," Theo said. "I'm so sorry."

Forty thousand dollars, a
betting app, then interest.
Theo was crying the way he did at fifteen,

when he thought I couldn't
hear through the wall.

His bookie works for Carmine
Brancato, who wants my port.

If you die before Thursday, with my name
in your statement, nobody needs a trial.

"So someone wants me
dead, and it isn't you."
It isn't me.
"Did you kill that man?"
I'm not going to answer that.
Marry me.

A wife can't be forced to
testify against her husband.
The privilege belongs to the wife.
Not to me. Not to Holloway.
I laughed. "I met you on Friday.
You bled on my shoes.
Here's my answer." I held up the subpoena.
"I'd rather testify."

Sunday, a man in bay seventeen
asked for the redheaded doctor.

In the supply room the door clicked shut
and IV tubing dropped over my head.

You get about ten seconds
before you pass out.
I teach that to students.

At five I drove my trauma shears into
the back of his hand, and he ran.

A huge man filled the doorway,
the quiet one with the crossword.
Rocco. "Go after him," I croaked.
"No, ma'am. My job's you."

That evening I stood by my car
with a red line round my throat.

I could become someone else
in a city I'd never seen,

or keep my work and my brother
and trust a man I didn't.
I was scared of him.
I was more scared of a plastic tube.
He answered on the first ring.
"I have conditions," I said.
His lawyer wrote it down in blue ink. One.
I keep my residency, every shift. Two.
My own bedroom, with a lock on my side.
Three. Theo's debt, gone tonight. Four.

No one in his family touches
me, including his men.
Five. When the case is dead, we divorce.
Six. Not one cent of his money.
"And seven. You never lie to me."
I'll never lie to you.
I won't always answer.
"That's a loophole."
That's the truth. You asked for the truth.
"Is it the only reason you want this?
If I can't testify, you're safe?"
No.
"What's the other one?"
He held my eyes and said nothing at all.
Beside him, Tommy looked at the table.
Whatever it was, Tommy knew.

My uncle Sal came at one-thirty with
a box of cannoli and sugar on his tie.

My father's brother, his consigliere
for twenty-five years, and now mine.

"You're a better man than
your father was," Sal said.
"But a better man makes trouble for himself.
A girl in the house with a federal subpoena.
It would be cleaner, Nico, the other way."
We don't touch civilians.

That's the only thing that makes
us different from Brancato.

Take that away and we're just
men with guns who like the port.
He held up both hands, cannoli in one.
"I had to say it so you could say no.

That's my job." Then he went out to the
garden for air and left the door open
behind him.
Eleven pages, typed overnight.

At the bottom of Nico's section, someone
had added a line by hand in big, shaky,
left-handed capitals.
She will look like she loves me.
I initialed it. I read every page twice.

The ring was his grandmother's,
a square emerald, far too big.
It slid around my finger.
"Rosa had big hands," he said.
"She made bread."

On the courthouse steps, eight
reporters and three cameras.
Holloway had been tipped.

Nico kissed me, slow and warm,
the plaster along my spine.
It was for the cameras.

For three seconds I forgot to count
anything, and I was angry about that all day.
Starting tonight, Dottoressa, we're in love.

He had put a bolt on my side of the
connecting door himself, at six that morning,
left-handed. The screws were crooked.
I tested it four times.

The ring was so loose it
kept turning to my palm.
Tuesday, the ER.
At work I couldn't wear a ring under gloves,

so I'd threaded his grandmother's emerald
onto a thin gold chain and tucked it
under my scrubs.

A wedding ring that lived
against my breastbone.

Joey, one of Nico's soldiers,
rolled in stabbed, lung collapsing.

I decompressed him and put in the tube
myself while mobsters watched me do it.
"Am I dead?" he asked. "Not on my shift."
In his jacket I found my whole October.

Every shift in blue ballpoint, small
neat slanted handwriting I didn't know.

And at the bottom,
underlined twice: Level 2.
Space 2-14.

Joey said the man who sent him
drove a car that smelled like anise.
Only the hospital had my schedule. Dr.

Bell had asked about my shifts
that morning, almost casually.

I told myself Bell asks
everybody everything.
I confronted Bell Thursday evening.
He cried.
His son Danny was seventeen and sick,

and the treatment cost four
hundred seventy thousand dollars.
A man had asked about my schedule.
Bell gave it.
I gave him until noon to call the FBI.
He asked for one more night. I said yes.

I have thought about that
yes every day since.
That night I was shaking, and he held me,

and he pulled the pen out of
my hair with his left hand.
I kissed him. He kissed me back.
I stopped. No cameras.
"That one wasn't for anyone," I said.
"Sleep," he said.
"I'll wake you at eleven."
At 6:41 Friday morning, Priya called. Dr.

Bell was dead in his Volvo,
three spaces from my spot.
A note on his phone. Suicide.
"Ivy, I'm sorry. I couldn't live with it.
Tell Danny I tried."

In three years Bell called
me Ivy maybe four times,
always when someone had just died.

In writing, always Marlowe,
even in his last text.

The note was a lie, and whoever
wrote it didn't know him.

Only four people had known
he'd talk to the FBI at noon.
Nico. Tommy. Rocco. And Nico's uncle Sal.

When I said that name aloud, Nico's eyes
dropped to the top drawer of his desk,
for as long as it takes to read a clock.
Sunday lunch under the fig.
Enzo excused himself and didn't come back.

I found him on his bathroom floor,
blue, a foil card beside him.
Oxycodone, thirty milligrams.
I breathed for him.
Two sprays of naloxone, three minutes apart.
He gasped.

I put the card in my cardigan
pocket before the paramedics came.
I only knew it mattered.

In the ER, Enzo grabbed my sleeve and
told me, because he thought he was dying.
"I shot him. I shot Frankie."

He had followed Frankie into the garage
and stood half a flight up the stairs,
holding his breath. A shoe scraped.
Frankie turned, and his gun came up.
Enzo fired twice and didn't even decide to.

Nico took the gun out of
his hand and told him to go.
Enzo was the light jacket on the stairs.

He had stopped when he
heard me ask for a tube.
Then he kept going.

I told him what he said in
that bay stays with me.
I didn't know yet what it would cost.
Then Theo was arrested.

Four hundred tablets, taped under
the driver's seat of his Civic.

Holloway offered a trade: my testimony
against Nico, and Theo walks.
Nico, in the car, never raised his voice.
"Do what you have to do.
I won't hate you."
I had my own evidence.
The sticker on Enzo's card said Lot 4471-B.
So did the pills in Theo's car.

I cornered the hospital pharmacy
director with an old committee letter.

Forty-two cards of that lot had been
"destroyed" on a form dated September
twenty-ninth, co-signed by Dr.
Marcus Bell. The tech said nobody counted.

The signing doctor carried the
bag out himself, past the garage.
Nico's people found the dealer.

His supplier was an old man in a gray
Lincoln that smelled of licorice.
Monday, Courtroom 6B.

Holloway wanted the judge
to call it a sham marriage.

He called me to the stand and
asked about the first week.
About the courthouse kiss.
And I invited him to ask the real question.
"Do you love your husband?"
"Yes. I love him.

And I'd like the record to show he's
hearing it for the first time with everyone
else."
The judge denied the motion from the bench.

She'd seen a great many sham marriages,
and none of them sounded like that.

In the car, Nico's left hand
lay open on the seat, palm up.
I put mine in it.

At my door he said, "One day, when
you're ready, and not before,
I'd like to hear it once without them."
At midnight I couldn't sleep.

Holloway had asked me that morning,
"Eleven pages?" Only I, Nico, Mr.

Feld and one copy in Nico's top drawer
knew how many pages the contract had.

Someone inside the house was
talking to the government's side.
I opened the drawer.

Under the paper, a white
twist of candy wrapper.
It smelled of anise.

One-ten in the morning,
in my uncle's garage.

I had found this car once before and told
myself Brancato might be framing him.
Half of Brooklyn sucks anise candy.
This time I opened the glove box.

A black ledger, its band off with my
teeth because I only had one hand.

C.B., every month for four years,
starting the week of my father's funeral.
And on the first of October: F.L. Twenty.
Paid.

In the trunk, a deli
receipt for a prepaid phone,
and a boy's tan jacket from a discount rack.

When I was eleven, my father broke my
nose, and Sal carried me out of that house.

She was sitting in my study with
the candy twist in her hand.
I said it before she could. It's my uncle.

At dawn, Danny Bell let me
read his father's last letter.

Marcus had signed the destruction form and
carried the pills to a gray car for cash.

Years ago he'd misdiagnosed a patient
who turned out to be Brancato's cousin,

and Brancato had held
it over him ever since.

The man in the gray car was
old, soft-spoken, nice coat.
The letter ended: Ivy, say it.
Say all of it.
Danny said I could give it to the FBI.
I gave Reyes everything except one name.

"Somebody else gets to
tell you first," I said.
Tuesday, seven p.m.

Sal arrived exactly on
time with a box of pastry.

Nico laid out the notebook,
the receipt, the jacket.
Sal didn't blink.

"Carmine wanted the port," he
said, "and the port was you.
Frankie lost his nerve.
I didn't know about the stairs.

I didn't know Carmine's boy
would send Enzo down them."
"Kids buy pills," he said.

"Better ours, from a hospital, clean, than
poison pressed in a bathtub in Jersey."
I broke my own rule and spoke.

"I breathed for your nephew
for four minutes, Mr.
Vescari. On your pills."

My father would have put
you in the water, Zio.
That's the answer I'm not giving anymore.
You'll go to Cefalù.

Everything you own goes to
Frankie's kids, Michael and Gina.
Sal looked at his hands, then at his nephew.

"Somebody in this family
had to be his father.
You were busy being a saint."

I put my phone on the tablecloth
and called Agent Reyes on speaker.
Sal almost smiled.
"Of course you called her, sweetheart.
You always do."

A day later I chained a deli receipt
and a pack of gum to Paulie Ferraro.
I called Reyes first, on purpose.
Then Nico.
Three weeks ago, I'd have sent Tommy.
I trust what you'd do.
Paulie confessed.
Theo walked out at 12:52.

In the car he said, "You never once asked
me if I wanted to be your kid." I'd been

so busy keeping him safe
that I'd never asked.
I asked.
Monday night Lucia found Enzo's room empty.
At 11:31 my phone rang. Carmine Brancato.

His own son had overdosed on
the floor of his club, and Enzo,

who'd walked in to offer himself for a
boy he'd hit on a bicycle four years ago,
had asked for the doctor.
I didn't ask permission.
I told everyone before, not after.
I texted Reyes. I went.
Enzo was already breathing for him.
I gave naloxone and bagged him.
Four minutes twenty seconds.
The boy coughed.

Brancato took a typed
statement out of his cardigan.

I, Enzo Vescari, state that
my brother ordered me to.
Enzo wouldn't sign it.
"I'll sign what's true.
I won't sign that."
I'm not armed, Carmine.
My wife doesn't like it.
Six guns turned.
I stepped in front of him. "Be quiet.

It's my turn." I told Brancato
what I'd tell a jury.
His son was breathing because of me.

If anyone fired, I would stand
in a courtroom and say who.

He said, "In my house, we don't point guns
at the doctor." He told them to put them
down.

Reyes came through the front door two
minutes later with a warrant signed at six.
She arrested Carmine Brancato.

I came in with nothing
because you were in that room.
That's the truth, Ivy.

Enzo turned himself in at
two-fourteen Tuesday morning.

In the visiting room I said,
I'm sorry I made you carry it,
and I cried in front of a guard.
Then I went to Holloway about the gun,

buried in the planter on Van
Brunt Street under the geraniums.

I told Feld to draw an uncontested
divorce and leave it on the hall table.

She gets to choose once
with nothing on the table.
That means I don't ask.
Thursday, third grand jury.

I waived my privilege
myself, that morning at six,
for October third and nothing else.
I told them what I saw. Two shots at 4:10.
A man sliding down a silver car.
A second gun near his open hand.

Nico standing over him with a gun in
his left hand, pointed at the floor,
held wrong, and his right hand in my splint.
"Did you see who fired?"
"No. I heard two shots.
I saw what was in his hands afterward."

Holloway told us in the hallway there'd
be no indictment for Frankie Lombardi:

Enzo's statement, my testimony,
Frankie's gun, the chart.
Nico would plead to tampering with a gun.

At two o'clock I took off the
splint, six weeks less one day.
His fist closed.
All of it, even the ring finger I sewed.
He looked at his own hand a long time.
Thank you, Dr. Marlowe.

That evening there was a cream
envelope on the hall table.
Term Five. Three stapled pages.
He'd signed it with his right hand, slowly,
like a man writing in a foreign language.
I put the papers down and went upstairs.
I didn't knock.

"Here's the thing about
the divorce," I said.

"I haven't asked." I emptied my cardigan
pockets onto his bed: Enzo's foil card,

the pharmacy form, his note,
Bell's envelope, a candy twist.
Everything I'd carried through five weeks.
I took the pen out of my hair.

On page eleven, under his
left-handed line, I wrote, She does.
And under that: Term six.
Nobody in this house is quiet anymore.

Last March a woman buried her son
from my house on Carroll Street.
Rosaria Amato.
She told me about a red-haired doctor at St.

Brigid's who sat with her
and told her the truth.
She said your name twice.

I read Marlowe on your badge,
and I chose that emergency room.
That was the other reason.
I love you, Ivy.

I've loved you since you put my money back
in my pocket and typed my name anyway.
April.
The lemon trees came out of their burlap.
"It's a lemon tree," Lucia said.
"It's Sicilian. It lives out of spite.

Like me." Theo has an apartment over a
laundromat and comes for Saturday lunch and
calls me Iv.

Enzo is in a program upstate,
a hundred forty-one days clean,

writing to his mother on Sundays and to a
boy named Anthony who hasn't answered yet.

Sal's letters from Cefalù,
Lucia burns unread.

Danny Bell is back at school; an
anonymous donor paid his treatment.

When I asked, Nico said, "I'm not
going to answer that," and smiled.
I finish residency in June.

Reyes came to the gate on
the first warm Saturday.

A motion from Brancato's
lawyers had surfaced old files.

Nico's father had been an
FBI informant for years.
Nico would read it in the Post by Friday.
I did not wait.
We don't do silence in this house anymore.
It's in the contract.

I climbed fourteen stairs,
counting every one,

to tell my husband the
truth about his father.
Two shots.
That's all it took to start all of this.
One yes, said out loud, is how it ended.
